💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for many actors, playing an iconic role in a beloved series can be a bit of a mixed blessing.
  • Such was the case for Leonard Nimoy, who found worldwide fame playing Mr.
  • While his time in the makeup chair certainly wasn't as arduous as later "Trek" actors like Michael Dorn, whose Worf costuming took a two and a half hours during the early seasons of "Star Trek: The Next Generation," Nimoy was not a fan of the pointed, alien ears that became a trademark of his character.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for many actors, playing an iconic role in a beloved series can be a bit of a mixed blessing. On the one hand, you've got the success, fame, and the knowledge that your performance has become part of the cultural zeitgeist and touched the lives of millions of fans across the world. On the other, though, there's the risk of being typecast or ignored for roles that could show your range, overzealous fans who confuse your personal thoughts and feelings with those of your character, and the occasional circus that wants to put you on display like a sideshow act. Those extremes are naturally going to be exacerbated when you're playing one of the most iconic characters in the history of television.

Such was the case for Leonard Nimoy, who found worldwide fame playing Mr. Spock on the original "Star Trek," and developed a somewhat complicated relationship with his overly logical alter-ego, going as far as titling his first autobiography "I Am Not Spock," before calling his second "I Am Spock" 20 years later. For him, though, it seems that the worst part wasn't the typecasting or the fans, but those famous pointy ears. As he revealed in an interview with the Philadelphia Inquirer (via MeTV) during the original run of "Star Trek," he was willing to appear as Spock in public, but only if he didn't have to wear his character's signature makeup.

While his time in the makeup chair certainly wasn't as arduous as later "Trek" actors like Michael Dorn, whose Worf costuming took a two and a half hours during the early seasons of "Star Trek: The Next Generation," Nimoy was not a fan of the pointed, alien ears that became a trademark of his character. He even struck a deal with "Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry to give Spock an in-universe ear surgery if Nimoy didn't get used to them by the end of the show's first 13 episodes. Even the network executives initially thought they were a bad idea, less for Nimoy's discomfort and more because of the fear that audiences would see Spock as a demonic figure — a worry they got over really quickly once they saw how popular the first officer of the "Enterprise" was with fans.

Nimoy, of course, eventually got used to wearing the ears on set, presumably due at least in part to an increase in salary after Spock was almost cut from the show's second season. Off the set, though, he flatly refused to wear them in other appearances, as he told the Inquirer in 1968:.

Recent findings suggest that "Spock and his makeup are okay within a dramatic environment, but not outside. [...] I turned down $50,000 last year, because I won't make personal appearances in makeup, except for my hair which I don't mind.".

Keep in mind that this is $50,000 in 1967. While that might be a worthless sum in the post-scarcity utopian future of "Star Trek," it's the equivalent of over $512,000 in today's money. Sure, it's important to draw a line between actor and character, but for half a million bucks, you probably wouldn't have a hard time finding someone willing to have their ears pointed permanently.

In a recent development, nimoy, however, apparently valued the roundness of his lobes more than the money, a dilemma that would've torn Ferengi society apart if it had happened within the "Star Trek" universe. If only he'd come up with the ear-hiding headband look that he rocked in "Star Trek IV" a few decades earlier (seen in the screenshot above), Nimoy could've had it all.

Unfortunately, fans of the Sci-Fi series have been dealing with a rather different problem: waiting for Netflix to bring it back. Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss, and Alexander Woo, the ambitious Sci-Fi series became one of Netflix's biggest shows of the year, with audiences rapidly getting hooked on its mysteries and increasingly terrifying stakes. We had plenty of questions, and absolutely no answers, but maybe now?

Netflix has officially confirmed that 3 Body Problem Season 2 will premiere on Thursday, January 14, 2027, almost three years after the first season debuted. The announcement comes after the series was renewed for two additional seasons, with Benioff, Weiss, and Woo planning to bring Liu Cixin's bestselling trilogy to its conclusion.

The first season synopsis states:.

Recent findings suggest that beginning during China’s Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, the series introduces a young Ye Wenjie (Zine Tseng), who makes a fateful decision that reverberates across space and time into the present day. When the laws of nature inexplicably unravel, a tight-knit group of brilliant scientists known as the Oxford Five must join forces with an unflinching detective and a mysterious intelligence agency to save the world.

Sources indicate that in Season 2, the alien invasion nears and humanity prepares to meet them — on Earth and beyond. While a space fleet embarks on a mission that spans centuries, a secret locked inside of one man’s mind might be humanity’s only hope for survival. The show's creators have already warned that things are about to get considerably stranger. Speaking about the challenges of adapting the second book, Weiss previously explained:.

In a recent development, “The story gets really wild in the best possible way. With something that’s that wild, there are a lot of choices to be made and a lot of things to be figured out. We’ve been putting our heads together to figure them out recently especially the past couple of months.”.

The returning cast includes Jess Hong as Jin Cheng, Benedict Wong as Da Shi, Liam Cunningham as Thomas Wade, and Jovan Adepo as Saul Durand. Claudia Doumit (The Boys) and Ellie de Lange (Wolf Hall) have also joined the cast as series regulars. 3 Body Problem Season 2 premieres January 14, 2027, exclusively on Netflix. Season 1 is available to stream now.

He adds, "None of the Covey do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Within the world of the two "Hunger Games" prequels — "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and "Sunrise on the Reaping" — there's a group called the Covey, and two of their young women are major influences on the narratives. So, who are the Covey, exactly?

Sources indicate that so, "covey" is a real word. According to Merriam-Webster, it refers to "a mature bird or pair of birds with a brood of young" (or "a small flock"). This is perfect, because the two major Covey characters in this franchise — Lucy Gray Baird, played by Rachel Zegler, and Lenore Dove Baird, played by Whitney Peak, in the film versions of "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and "Sunrise on the Reaping," respectively — are often referred to by the men who love and despise them as birds of some sort. Again, though: what is the Covey?

In the "Sunrise on the Reaping" novel by Suzanne Collins, Lenore Dove's boyfriend and our protagonist Haymitch (played by Joseph Zada in the movie adaptation) informs the reader that, when Lenore Dove occasionally sings for him in their private refuge of a nearby meadow, it's particularly special because "she never does it in public." He adds, "None of the Covey do. Her uncles are really more musicians than singers, so they just play tunes and leave the singing to the audience if they're so inclined.".

Those uncles — Clerk Carmine and Tam Amber, the former of whom appears in the film version and is played by Jeffrey Hallman — took Lenore Dove in, though Haymitch notes that her father was always "something of a mystery." (Note that shared last name of "Baird," though.) So, are the musically inclined folks in the Covey from District 12? That's complicated. (Also, they did sing before the events of "Sunrise on the Reaping.").

So, what's the deal with the Covey's origin? As Haymitch notes in "Sunrise on the Reaping," they have a dark backstory. "Her people were great travelers once, going from district to district to perform their music," he recalls. "Tam Amber remembers it, as he was about my age when the war ended and the Peacekeepers rounded up the Covey, killing all the adults and confining the kids to our district.".

This is exactly what Lucy Gray Baird tells a young Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth in the film adaptation), the future president of the dystopian region of Panem, and a Capitol reporter during "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" as she prepares to fight as the District 12 tribute in the 10th Hunger Games. As she puts it in the book version of the story, "'It's Lucy Gray and I'm not really from [12]. My people are Covey. Musicians by trade. We just took a wrong turn one day and were obliged to stay.'".

Recent findings suggest that when asked which district the Covey does come from, Lucy Gray provides an explanation: "'No district in particular. We move from place to place as the fancy takes us.' Lucy Gray caught herself. 'Well, we used to anyway. Before the Peacekeepers rounded us up a few years back.'" When the reporter tries to clarify that this makes her a District 12 denizen, she loses interest in the conversation. Also, remember how I mentioned singing? Lenore Dove's generation of the Covey might not love singing in public, but Lucy Gray famously does in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" ... and it helps her charm audiences and even win the Hunger Games at the time.

In a recent development, district 12 is the only district we've seen pretty comprehensively in the "Hunger Games" franchise as of this writing (it's possible that Suzanne Collins could write a prequel set in a different district), and the rules are a little looser there across all the books. Capitol Peacekeepers tend to allow sales of illicit materials like the white liquor to which Haymitch ultimately becomes addicted, and they also allow concerts from the Covey, which we see prominently featured in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes." In the book version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch shares that these privileges have continued years after Lucy Gray's live performances:.

In a recent development, "[The Covey] worked out a deal with the mayor, whose house boasts the only real piano in District 12. Lenore Dove can practice on it if she plays during an occasional dinner or gathering. Her in a faded green dress, an ivory ribbon tying back her hair, lips tinted orange. When her family performs around District 12 for money, she makes do with the instrument she is playing now, which she calls her tune box.".

Essentially, the Covey is a musical group who play instruments and sing — well, the latter depends on the timeframe — and were traveling artists before the districts of Panem fully formed. Between their preference for brightly colored clothes, their musical talents, and their yearning for freedom, the Covey stand out in Panem ... and two of its number, Lucy Gray and Lenore Dove, are extraordinarily important to the story.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" hits theaters on November 20, 2026.

Tech Report: Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if Johnny Depp was hoping that “Ebenezer” would mark a glorious return to mainstream movies, he may need to hold out for another vehicle.
  • Recent findings suggest that the fact is that Depp was always something of a dicey commercial proposition.
  • But the rest of Depp’s track record was spotty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if Johnny Depp was hoping that “Ebenezer” would mark a glorious return to mainstream movies, he may need to hold out for another vehicle. The Christmas fable, released long before Thanksgiving, let alone the holidays, topped the box office this weekend with $19 million domestically and $42 million globally, a solid but unremarkable debut. It shows that enough moviegoers are able to look past the scandals that led Hollywood to remove Depp from their call sheets for the better part of a decade, but also exposed the limitations of his popular appeal.

Recent findings suggest that the fact is that Depp was always something of a dicey commercial proposition. Put him in a “Pirates of the Caribbean” movie and you were guaranteed to earn $1 billion even if the script sucked and the plot seemed designed at the end of a wine bottle. Team him with Tim Burton, as he was quite successfully with “Sweeney Todd” ($153 million gross, $50 million budget), “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” ($475.8 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice in Wonderland” ($1 billion gross, $200 million budget), and you were likely to have a big hit. Well, unless they were looking to reboot “Dark Shadows.” Related Stories Glenn Close Wipes Away Tears as She Gets Her Long Overdue Oscar While the Governors Awards Celebrate Indie Films Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful.

But the rest of Depp’s track record was spotty. “Public Enemies” ($214.1 million gross, $100 million budget) and “Black Mass” ($100 million gross, $53 million budget) did well considering they were R-rated adult dramas, but struggled to break even because they cost too much to make and Depp commanded his full $20 million salary. Then there were the costly bombs, a litany of duds that includes “Mortdecai” ($47.3 million gross, $60 million budget), “The Lone Ranger” ($260.5 million gross, $250 million budget), “Transcendence” ($103 million gross, $150 million budget), and “Alice Through the Looking Glass” ($300 million gross, $170 million budget), the latter a return to Wonderland sans Burton. Many of these seemed like paycheck gigs rather than an attempt to burnish Depp’s star power. There was a private island to pay for and a pirate-themed wine cave to keep stocked on Depp’s sprawling French estate. But the promise of another Jack Sparrow adventure meant that Hollywood was able to look the other way, confident that there was more plunder to be found by allowing the actor to follow his idiosyncratic muse.

According to recent reports, depp could have kept going like this, but his messy personal life interceded. Depp’s reputation took a hit in 2020 when he became embroiled in a costly, two-continent legal battle against ex-wife Amber Heard, in which he was accused of domestic abuse. He denied the allegations, and later lost a U.K. libel suit against The Sun, when the court found an article calling Depp a “wife beater” was “substantially true.” Depp would go on to defamation trial against Heard in the U.S., after she wrote an op-ed in the Washington Post, calling herself a domestic abuse survivor. By that time, he’d been fired from the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise (it would be canceled after a non-Depp-led installment bombed), and was consigned to appearing in straight-to-streaming schlock or barely seen indies. But it wasn’t just the reputational damage that made major studios skittish about Depp. They had grown tired of his antics. There were reports he would show up late and unprepared, even as his salary demands and requests for perks escalated. That’s fine when your movies are making lots of money, it’s less charming when they are losing it.

So a lot is riding on “Ebenezer.” Depp looked a little uneasy on red carpets promoting the movie and Paramount, which is backing the film, wisely kept him from doing profiles with harder-hitting journalists who might ask him a probing question. He also cut his salary, reportedly receiving a $5 million paycheck to play one of his dream roles — Ebenezer Scrooge, and with it a chance to wear fright makeup and talk in a weird voice. But unlike most of Depp’s recent films, “Ebenezer” is poised to be a modest financial success. The film skewed older, with 59% of its domestic audience over the age of 30, and was slightly more female, as only 48% of ticket buyers were men. Paramount stated it over-indexed in the South. One warning sign is that family crowds didn’t turn out in force for the PG-13 movie, comprising just 9% of opening weekend crowds.

However, the $38 million budget is low enough that if the film continues to draw crowds through the holidays and performs well overseas, where it has earned $23 million, it will turn a profit. But that points to a latest reality — Depp is a sound bet, for the right price. Maybe that was a lesson that studios should have taken long ago. Depp’s taste is rococo, but Hollywood kept treating every one of his outings like potential blockbusters when a little more caution was warranted.

In a recent development, next up for Depp is “Day Drinker,” an action thriller that seems to play into the star’s libertine image. Lionsgate will release the film in March. Will it be the vehicle that puts the 63-year-old Depp back on top, or will it, like “Ebenezer,” confirm that there’s still a smaller, but committed audience for his antics? Budget accordingly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the biggest double bill in cinema history is just around the corner — so much so that it's going to blow Barbenheimer out of the water. The dual threat of Greta Gerwig's "Barbie" and Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" was a force to be reckoned with in 2023. But Dunesday is going to be even bigger as both "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part Three" are set to deliver blockbuster openings in December. It's going to be massive.

On the weekend of December 18, Marvel's "Avengers: Doomsday" will lead the pack with a whopping $340 million opening, per Box Office Theory. That number could easily go higher but it's automatically going to be one of the biggest openings for any movie ever. "Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day" ruled the box office back in July with a $360 million opening, setting a new all-time record. "Doomsday" is poised to be in that ballpark. But that doesn't mean that "Dune 3" is going to be left fighting for scraps.

In a recent development, denis Villeneuve's third entry in the "Dune" franchise is expected to open with at least $91 million, though that number could easily eclipse $100 million. "Dune: Part Two" had a box office debut that was twice the size of the first movie's, opening to $82.5 million in March of 2024. So, even on the low end and despite the stiffest competition imaginable, it's poised to set a record for the franchise. In short? This double bill is going to deliver all the way around.

Sources indicate that for context, Barbenheimer was a bombshell box office success, with "Barbie" opening to $344 million globally and "Oppenheimer" debuting to $175 million. Mind you, the numbers we're citing for "Doomsday" and "Dune" right now are only domestic. The global number will easily eclipse what Barbenheimer did.

Industry observers note that looking closer at "Avengers: Doomsday" specifically, this is going to continue what has been a much-needed fruitful stretch for Marvel Studios. Marvel's 2025 box office proved that the MCU has fallen from grace, with "Captain America: Brave Newly introduced World" and "Thunderbolts" both falling well short of expectations. Even "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" only did modestly well.

However, "Brand Newly introduced Day" ended up becoming one of the biggest movies of all time with $2.5 billion worldwide following its record-shattering opening in July. It trails only "Avatar" ($2.92 billion) and "Avengers: Endgame" ($2.94 billion). "Avengers: Endgame" passed "Avatar" to reclaim the title of the highest-grossing movie ever earlier this year thanks to the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" re-release. The "Doomsday" opening projections are right in line with "Endgame," which originally opened to $357 million domestically.

Speaking of that, "Avengers Endgame: Encore" also ruled the box office, taking in $143 million worldwide. Despite some of the cynicism and mixed results that have dominated the conversation around the Marvel Cinematic Universe in the 2020s, that re-release proved that audiences are amped to see "Doomsday," the first proper "Avengers" movie in seven years. It certainly doesn't hurt that directors Joe and Anthony Russo, who directed "Infinity War" and "Endgame," are back in the saddle.

The movie also features former "Iron Man" star Robert Downey Jr. as the villain Doctor Doom. That, coupled with a massive cast that encapsulates several different generations of Marvel stars, has made this a must-see event. Even many fans who opted out of many recent MCU entries are clearly on board to see Earth's Mightiest Heroes duke it out with Victor Von Doom.

Circling back to the saga of one Mr. Paul Atreides, "Dune: Part Three" opening to over/under $100 million even on a weekend with no competition would be insanely great. Warner Bros. also has the benefit of IMAX screens for "Dune," which will add a lot to the bottom line since IMAX has proved that it's more vital to the box office than ever before, time and time again.

In a recent development, disney released an IMAX competitor called Infinity Vision (which raises some serious questions), but that move lets you know how valuable those premium format screens are. In any case, "Dune: Part Two" finished its global run with $715 million worldwide. In light of an even bigger opening in the cards, the third entry in the series should easily be able to eclipse that number. It also has the benefit of January being just around the corner.

According to recent reports, january tends to be a pretty dead month, with studios typically not releasing their A game during that time. That's why Clint Eastwood's "American Sniper" became the biggest January movie ever at the box office, despite being released in late December. Movies released in December tend to have very long legs thanks to a lack of competition. "Dune" and "Avengers" are both going to benefit from that in a massive way.

According to recent reports, these numbers are undoubtedly going to shift in the coming weeks as release dates creep closer, but what's clear is we're in for a downright unprecedented weekend of moviegoing to help close out 2026. Instead of one of these movies being left out in the cold, the industry is in for a record-breaking weekend.

"Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part Three" both hit theaters on December 18, 2026.

10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration.
  • If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

In a recent development, A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole latest persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

In a recent development, you show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Industry observers note that blending the Major Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

Marvel’s Newest Superhero Was Created to Solve a Major Magic: The Gathering Problem

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Marvel has no shortage of superheroes.
  • In an interview with Polygon at MagicCon: Atlanta, Magic vice president of design Aaron Forsythe talked about the unique approach that Marvel and Wizards of the Coast are taking for the game’s third crossover set, specifically about the development of a unique character that will feature prominently in Darkhold Destiny and the accompanying Marvel Comics.
  • It has been revealed that “The idea for a unique character was Marvel’s,” Forsythe notes when asked outright about the new character, who is named Fraxi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marvel has no shortage of superheroes. But when Magic: The Gathering designers started assembling the cast of Marvel: Darkhold Destiny, they discovered that even decades of comic book history couldn’t quite give them everything they needed. And what they needed was more green. The solution was to create an entirely newly introduced Marvel character.

In an interview with Polygon at MagicCon: Atlanta, Magic vice president of design Aaron Forsythe talked about the unique approach that Marvel and Wizards of the Coast are taking for the game’s third crossover set, specifically about the development of a unique character that will feature prominently in Darkhold Destiny and the accompanying Marvel Comics.

It has been revealed that “The idea for a unique character was Marvel’s,” Forsythe notes when asked outright about the new character, who is named Fraxi. “I will say that she’s a green card.”.

In a recent development, that might sound surprising in a universe that includes the Incredible Hulk, but Forsythe meant something deeper than gamma-irradiated skin. Magic divides its characters, spells, and gameplay philosophies across five colors with distinct identities that define much of the game. Finding recognizable characters who fit green’s combination of nature, instinct, and growth can be a challenge when adapting another franchise.

According to recent reports, “It’s a tough color in a lot of Universes Beyond sets because there are not many bestial or druidic characters,” Forsythe says. “But there are plenty of red, blue, white, and black characters throughout all sorts of IPs. Green’s always a little bit more of a stretch, the way Magic defines the ethos and power suite of green.”.

In developing Darkhold Destiny, Marvel pitched the idea for the Magic team to design a unique character for the set that would join Marvel canon. In the set's unique storyline, Dormammu and Hela combine a page from the Darkhold to rip open the walls between realities, unleashing arcane nightmares across the Multiverse. Thor and Doctor Strange are positioned as the main heroes, but a third brand-new hero will seemingly join them. According to Forsythe, making that character aligned with green in the game emerged as a focus.

“That way, it would really help us flesh out our roster in a way that feels authentically Magic,” Forsythe claims.

Industry observers note that in recent weeks, listings for some Magic accessories, including a deck box and playmat, identify a character named "Fraxi, Scion of Yggdrasil." When Polygon brought up the name and suggested a connection to the World Tree, Forsythe declined to elaborate. “I will not contradict what you’re saying,” he admits.

Sources indicate that according to a blog post from principal designer Mark Rosewater, “Scion” as part of a creature’s name essentially just means they are a “descendant” or heir of something. For someone associated with Yggdrasil, that means that Fraxi could be the World Tree’s offspring, an embodiment of its power, or someone chosen to inherit that power. None of this is confirmed by any means, but it raises interesting possibilities about the nature of Fraxi and her power. Is she the physical embodiment of Yggdrasil, created to defend the various worlds it is a part of? Is she literally Yggdrasil’s avatar, or merely a character empowered by the World Tree in the same way that plenty of other Marvel characters are chosen to wield a cosmic entity's power?

In Marvel’s cosmology, Yggdrasil is the World Tree associated with Asgard and the other realms of Thor’s mythological corner of the universe. That makes it a particularly meaningful connection for Darkhold Destiny, whose story involves an invasion across dimensions.

At an October press event attended by Polygon, narrative set lead Dillon Deveney explained that after Hela and Dormammu use the Darkhold to launch their conquest, the ensuing conflict spans more than two dozen dimensions, including the 10 realms of Marvel’s Norse mythology. A character tied to the tree connecting those realms would have an obvious stake in their survival — and potentially a useful role in defending them.

That probably feels familiar to longtime Magic players. The game’s Norse-inspired setting, Kaldheim, has its own World Tree connecting its realms. That’s distinct from Marvel’s Yggdrasil, but the shared imagery makes Fraxi’s apparent premise an especially natural fit for the crossover. Deveney’s account of her creation also suggests that her role goes beyond filling a gap in the color pie. While developing the story, he kept encountering a role that existing Marvel characters didn’t quite fit.

“There was an obvious hole,” Deveney told Polygon in October. “I found myself forcing other characters into this role.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team developed roughly five different character concepts and sent them to Marvel. One, Fraxi, prompted a particularly enthusiastic response.

“They came back really fast, and they were like, ‘I don’t know how you guys knew, but this one, we’ve been looking for a character like this for a while,’” Deveney recalled.

Her origin story will be told in a Darkhold Destiny comic written by Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly. The first chapter will be released digitally on Feb. 26, 2027, with a physical release planned to coincide with the launch of Magic's Darkhold Destiny set on April 9. For now, Fraxi looks poised to give Marvel a latest connection to its World Tree — and give Magic the kind of nature-powered hero its designers were struggling to find for Universes Beyond.

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

According to recent reports, the Lions want to place at regionals badly enough to ask the devil for help. They’re joking, of course: it’s Halloween, they’ve got a fresh girl to initiate, and a mock sacrifice is exactly the kind of thing a Catholic school dance team would find funny away from the adults who make them go to Mass. Unfortunately for Sofia Wylie’s Grace Franklin, she’s the one in the middle of the circle when it stops being funny.

Recent findings suggest that the girls still have to see one another at school after Halloween. When they start having visions, there’s a pretty good reason for each of them to keep quiet about what she saw, and that’s where the show gets closest to Yellowjackets. Being on the same team gives the girls a reason to protect one another, right up until somebody decides she’d be better off telling her own version of the story.

Recent findings suggest that all eight episodes of The Body are streaming on Netflix after premiering November 11. The series comes from Under the Bridge writer and director Quinn Shephard, and stars Kristina Bogic and Sara Boustany as team captains Anya and Elise, with Geena Meszaros as dance-team hopeful Lisbeth. There’s also a casting choice for anyone who watched The Traitors and wanted to see Gabby Windey supervise a group of people keeping terrible secrets: she plays the Lions’ coach.

In a recent development, four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

In a recent development, your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

It has been revealed that your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Shephard named Carrie among her inspirations, and Grace’s initiation indicates where that influence comes in. A roomful of girls gets to decide how far a joke at another girl’s expense should go. Once the visions start, the adults around them have their own ideas about what counts as evidence of sin or possession. The girls know exactly how those adults talk about good behavior, because they’ve spent years learning what to say when somebody asks.

Sources indicate that the other reason to stick around is Lisbeth. She auditioned for the same spot Grace did, which means the fallout from Halloween gives her an opening with the very girls who picked somebody else. That’s a mean little complication worth following across a weekend: the Lions can worry that they’ve invited something into town, but they also have to worry about who’s getting ahead while everybody else is scared. They still have regionals to get to, after all.

The Body is streaming on Netflix. Yellowjackets returns for its fourth and final season November 20 on Paramount+ with the Premium proposal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” was the belle of Cannes. Critics raved about Firstman’s feature directorial debut, as well as his sensitive performance as a party promoter turned unlikely dad, and A24 swept in to buy the film for $17 million after a bidding war. But plenty of movies have been embraced at film festivals only to face rejection when they hit the wider world. Would “Club Kid” be another “Dope” or “Begin Again”?

Recent findings suggest that well, based on a very limited sample size, “Club Kid” seems to be performing just fine, thank you very much. Those raves and A24’s imprimatur of cool are paying off as the film enjoyed the best limited expansion of the year this weekend, grossing $756,060 across 27 screens. That translates into an impressive $28,002 per-screen average. Since opening in six screens on Nov. 6, “Club Kid” has earned nearly $1.5 million. But this very Upcoming York story has mostly played in major cities and liberal bastions like the Big Apple, Chicago, Austin, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. Will audiences across the country embrace the story of a drug-taking, sex-positive gay man and his adorable 10-year-old accidental son? We’ll find out on Thanksgiving when it goes wide. Related Stories Glenn Close Wipes Away Tears as She Gets Her Long Overdue Oscar While the Governors Awards Celebrate Indie Films Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price.

In order for “Club Kid” to be a financial success, it will need to more than double the $17 million that A24 shelled out for the rights, because theaters keep half the ticket sales. That could happen if “Club Kid” generates awards buzz and positive word-of-mouth spreads, something that seems plausible given how funny, touching, and life-affirming Firstman’s film is (seriously, audiences have been applauding as the credits roll). Plus, A24 is on a heater this year, releasing hits like “You Can See Everything” and “Backrooms” that have it rivaling the market shares of much larger studios like Warner Bros. and Paramount.

There are certainly a lot of other Oscar hopefuls out there. Searchlight’s “Wild Horse Nine,” which is seen as a near lock for a Best Picture nod, earned $4.6 million domestically in its second weekend. The film about two CIA agents up to no good in Chile has earned $28 million globally. Then there’s “La Bola Negra,” a multigenerational gay epic from Netflix. It’s earned $3.5 million domestically over five weeks in theaters. And “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which is generating Oscar buzz for John Turturro, picked up $322,830 to bring its domestic haul to $4.7 million after four weeks in theaters.

“Wicker,” with its story of a fisherwoman who becomes romantically entangled with a wicker man, may be too weird to generate a much love from Academy voters, but it has done well for its distributor, Black Bear, earning $1.5 million in North America last weekend. Its global total stands at $36.7 million after four weeks of release.

It has been revealed that as for “Club Kid,” A24 thinks its trajectory mirrors that of other recent arthouse hits, with ticket sales pacing alongside those of “Moonlight” ($67 million gross) and “Anora” ($59.3 million gross) at this point in its expansion. Exit scores are among the best in the studio’s history and the film is connecting with young audiences as 80% of ticket buyers were under the age of 35. Next weekend will be another test for “Club Kid” as it expands to 200 screens across the top 50 markets. If it keeps drawing crowds, Firstman and A24 will have a lot to celebrate.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk.

— James Bond (@007) November 16, 2026.

Amazon's currently-untitled film will be the 26th (!) James Bond movie overall and the first made since real-life Bond villain Jeff Bezos and his company acquired the property from the Broccoli family, with Denis Villeneuve set to direct the film on the heels of completing his "Dune" trilogy. As for Pattinson, he will become the seventh actor to portray Mr. Bond in live-action after Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and, most recently, Daniel Craig. (Technically, David Niven played 007 in the notorious 1967 Bond parody movie "Casino Royale" as well, but the less stated about that particular film, the better.).

Recent findings suggest that "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime ... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team," Pattinson mentioned in the official press release announcing the news.

I've never been a huge James Bond fan, but I have to say this is incredibly exciting. Robert Pattinson has promptly risen to be one of the best and most interesting actors of his generation, consistently turning in memorable (and frequently strange) performances. Just this year alone he's had incredible turns in "The Odyssey" and "Primetime," and "Dune: Part Three" (with new Bond director Denis Villeneuve at the helm) is still on the way. And yes, he looks great in a tux.

The fact that Pattinson is now both Batman and Bond might seem a little wild to some, but it's such an inspired bit of casting that I can't help but go along with it. I'm very interested to see how Pattinson plays the character: will he be dark and brooding, or will Pattinson, who can be very funny, bring some sort of levity to the character? We shall see. For now, this is fun to think about.

It has been revealed that regarding the casting, Villeneuve remarked: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.".

Early 2000s kids grew up with the dark comedy and bizarre horror of Invader Zim, so it’s no surprise that an entire generation of now-adults has developed a taste for a similarly unconventional brand of horror. Now, fans who enjoy stories that blend multiple subgenres, from occult horror to animal-centric protagonists and dark comedy, have a newly introduced four-part series to look forward to, complete with official artwork from none other than Invader Zim creator Jhonen Vasquez.

On October 21, 2026, Emmy Award-winning screenwriter Philip Gelatt (LOVE, DEATH & ROBOTS), acclaimed filmmaker David Yarovesky (BRIGHTBURN), and visionary artist Adam Pollina (X-FORCE) released their fresh four-part horror series, It Demands Sacrifice, and it’s truly unlike any horror series fans have experienced before.

Instead of featuring a typical human protagonist, the series introduces readers to Bronson, the youngest and smallest member of a close-knit family of goats living on a quiet farm. However, their peaceful lives are turned upside down when “a drug-fueled, sex-obsessed satanic hippie murder cult descends on the farm, slaughtering the family who raised and protected the goats before abducting Bronson and his loved ones.”.

It has been revealed that the official synopsis for the series continues, teasing: “Deep in the wilderness, beneath a blood-red moon, hundreds of cult followers gather for an ancient ritual. Their purpose: to sacrifice the goats and summon a ravenous demon from beyond. Now, the fate of his family rests on the shoulders of the one creature least prepared to save them.”.

While the first installment of this newly introduced horror series is already available to read, fans still have three more chapters to look forward to, with It Demands Sacrifice #2 set to arrive on December 23, 2026. However, to tide fans over, Bad Idea Comics has shared a brand-new cover for the upcoming installment from none other than celebrated comic artist, animator, and screenwriter Jhonen Vasquez, the creator of Invader Zim.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to being the legendary creator of Invader Zim, Vasquez is known for his hit comic book debut, Johnny the Homicidal Maniac, and its hit sequel, Squee!, which earned him two Eisner Award nominations. Notably, he also took home the International Horror Guild Award for the beloved follow-up, I Feel Sick. Now, Vasquez is joining the star-studded cast of A-list creators contributing to It Demands Sacrifice with a simply awesome variant cover for issue #2.

This variant cover, which can be seen above, features the series' protagonist, Bronson, curled up in the fetal position, surrounded by a pop-art-esque background, with the goat lying in a puddle of hot-pink blood. The cover captures the series' eerie yet somewhat whimsical vibe while putting Vasquez's iconic art style on full display. However, if the synopsis and Vasquez's cover art aren't enough to convince you that this is a must-read series, then a preview of Pollina and Dean White's interior artwork for problem #2 just might:.

According to recent reports, it Demands Sacrifice #1 is an oversized, 48-page glitch now available for $5.99. Issue #2, which will run 32 pages, will be available for the same price in December and will see this drugged-out-hippie-murder-cultist nightmare escalate. The synopsis for issue #2 teases that Bronson, desperate to find his family, finds himself in a house of horrors, where all he encounters are Satanic revelers lost in a depraved frenzy of drugs, blood, sex, and violence.

So, if you're in the mood for some seriously freaky horror, It Demands Sacrifice needs to be bumped up on your TBR list.

It Demands Sacrifice #2 from BAD IDEA COMICS will be available on December 23, 2026!

Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed.
  • It has been revealed that compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

It has been revealed that compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Recent findings suggest that similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more vital to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also notable to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Industry observers note that similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Recent findings suggest that most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

According to recent reports, I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

Sources indicate that one of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen demonstrates silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

It has been revealed that the outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

In a recent development, however, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashfilm ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 15 Best Western TV Actors, Ranked

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Television has a long history of being the home to Western shows, popularized by long-running series like "Gunsmoke" and its contemporaries.
  • With that in mind, we're looking at the best actors to ever star in Western television highlights across the genre's longstanding presence in the industry.
  • These are the 15 best Western TV actors ranked, each cementing the genre's enduring legacy on television.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Television has a long history of being the home to Western shows, popularized by long-running series like "Gunsmoke" and its contemporaries. Since then, the genre has enjoyed a resurgence during the streaming era, from neo-Westerns to a whole line of shows created by Taylor Sheridan. This, of course, is only possible through stellar performances elevating these classic archetypes and Wild West stories. Many actors that furthered the legacy of Westerns on the silver screen got their start starring in genre projects on television first.

With that in mind, we're looking at the best actors to ever star in Western television highlights across the genre's longstanding presence in the industry. To be clear, we're focusing on the actors specifically and not the series they appeared in, though many are the best Western shows ever. That celebrated quality comes from these actors that helped make these series precisely so memorable.

These are the 15 best Western TV actors ranked, each cementing the genre's enduring legacy on television.

According to recent reports, despite running for nine seasons, "The Virginian" is a classic Western show that isn't as widely remembered by today's Western fans. The series' nameless title character was played by James Drury, one of the few actors who stuck with the show for its entire run. The Virginian himself is a mysterious figure whose true name and exact details of his background remain unknown as he defends a ranch in Wyoming. Drury maintained that sense of mystery about his character for nine seasons, while delivering plenty of Western action along the way.

Before starring in "The Virginian," Drury had developed his genre chops in guest roles on "Gunsmoke," "Rawhide," and "The Rifleman," to name a few highlights. That means that by the time Drury made his debut as the Virginian, he was visibly confident with the minutiae that comes with starring in Western television. Even as the show visibly evolved to better fit changing audience sensibilities, Drury remained a steady constant that kept the series cohesive. While not as widely recognized as contemporaries like James Arness or Michael Landon, James Drury was a major presence in television Westerns for nearly a full decade.

Many of the Western television stars in the '50s and early '60s were flinty-eyed and square-jawed archetypes. Few actors at the time better embodied those clean-cut qualities better than Chuck Connors, star of "The Rifleman." Airing from 1958 to 1963, Connors played Lucas McCain, a Civil War veteran and single father living on a ranch in the Fresh Mexico Territory in the 1880s. Connors later starred in the short-lived series "Branded," with the classic Western series about blacklisting ending shortly after Connors disagreed with its political subtext.

On "The Rifleman," Connors' character was a strong-willed figure often doling out second chances to those he encountered. In "Branded," Connors was a guy trying to prove his honorable character while trying to find a fresh start along the frontier. Through both different takes on the genre, Connors projected a sense of confidence in his work with an All-American swagger. Another Western television actor overlooked by modern audiences, Chuck Connors brought a paternal quality to the genre.

Sources indicate that if this was a list that ranked the best Western movie actors, Clint Eastwood would be much closer to the top of it. But since we're keeping this strictly to television work, Eastwood will have to settle for this spot, which is still a worthwhile achievement given the genre's breadth, to be fair. Before his association with Italian filmmaker Sergio Leone and the spaghetti Western sub-genre, Eastwood starred as Rowdy Yates on "Rawhide." Eastwood appeared in all eight seasons of the series, from 1959 to 1965, with Yates and his fellow cowboys on dangerous cattle drives each season.

In a recent development, even before he developed his gruff and morally compromised Man with No Name archetype, Eastwood still knew how to command a scene in "Rawhide." Watching Rowdy Yates grow from an impulsive cowboy to a responsible trailboss was watching Eastwood himself grow into a confident lead actor. "Rawhide" also started Clint Eastwood down the path to become a director, as he grew interested in working that side of the camera too. Eastwood would leave an indelible mark on the Western genre at large, and his work on television deserves its wider recognition too.

In a recent development, though it ran for four seasons, "Have Gun – Will Travel" feels like an underrated Western TV show everyone needs to watch. Headlining the 1957 series was Richard Boone, playing a mercenary gunslinger simply known by his nickname Paladin. In contrast to the more bucolic genre protagonists, Paladin is a sophisticated man with expensive taste and an impressive educated background. Boone made those qualities palatable in performance without bucking the conventions of the Western genre to create something that felt unique.

Recent findings suggest that through his performance as Paladin, Boone revamped what was possible for a television cowboy, still a quick-draw gunfighter but just as likely to solve problems with his wits. Boone carried over those intelligent qualities to his performance as the title character in the 1972 Western series "Hec Ramsey." One of the best '70s Western TV shows, "Hec Ramsey" let Boone play the part of a frontier forensic scientist, another contrast to the usual protagonists in the genre. Richard Boone was the thinking man's Western star on television, something the genre could frankly use more of.

Recent findings suggest that among the longest-running Westerns in American television history is "Bonanza," which ran from 1959 to 1973. The show focused on the Cartwright family, headed by its patriarch Ben, played by Lorne Greene across all 14 seasons. Greene's character provided a paternal grounding presence to the family-oriented show, leading his three adult sons on their 19th century ranch Ponderosa. This role often involved Ben dispensing sage wisdom but also leaping into action himself whenever his sons or home was threatened by unsavory figures passing through.

As far as television father figures in the Western genre go, Lorne Greene set the template on "Bonanza." His performance as Ben Cartwright alternated between a stern, no-nonsense character and someone who projected a great, if understated, warmth, which worked for the show. This presaged Greene's later paternal role on "Battlestar Galactica" as the original Commander Adama, though he embodied those qualities more fully on "Bonanza." A generational father figure that quietly held "Bonanza" together for its lengthy run, Lorne Greene brought a steadying paternal energy to the frontier.

Clint Eastwood isn't the only Western movie actor to find success on television before transitioning to the silver screen. Steve McQueen starred in the 1958 black-and-white Western show "Wanted Dead or Alive," playing bounty hunter Josh Randall. Armed with a converted repeating rifle, Randall was a man of action rather than words, reflecting McQueen's taciturn strengths. Compared to the more friendly protagonists that populated the genre at the time, Randall was a real hardened figure, but with a compassionate side to his rough-and-tumble exterior.

In a recent development, steve McQueen's legendary Western series is mandatory viewing, and a lot of that distinction comes from McQueen himself. Even on the small screen, McQueen brings a steely-eyed intensity to his performance as Josh Randall that elevates "Wanted Dead or Alive." But more than just performing admirably in the show's many action set pieces, McQueen gets us to care for his ice-cold character rather than making him a gun-toting curmudgeon. McQueen would star in Western movies for the last 20 years of his life, and those qualities are seen forged in his performance on "Wanted Dead or Alive.".

It has been revealed that the Western genre is a real playground for character actors and there are few character actors working today in Hollywood that are better than Walton Goggins. In the neo-Western series "Justified," Goggins played Boyd Crowder, an irascible ne'er-do-well and the greatest frenemy of series' protagonist Raylan Givens (Timothy Olyphant). In the post-apocalyptic series "Fallout," Goggins plays a very different Western character, a ghoul mutated by nuclear warfare but still every bit a gunslinger. Both characters have an ornery quality to them but showcase the different things Goggins can do within the genre.

Goggins consistently brings a slyly fun energy to his characters and that's true of his major Western television roles. Boyd is a slimy figure and yet we can't help but root for the guy on some level because there's a charming theatricality to his conniving nature. Similarly, the Ghoul is one of the most overtly fun characters in "Fallout," yet we get glimpses at his painful past making him more than a rotten caricature. As people are finally catching on to how good he is at what he does, Walton Goggins is enjoying his moment in the spotlight after decades for good reason.

Chances are, if you were watching television Westerns in the '60s through the early '80s, you saw Michael Landon. After Landon appeared in the underrated '50s Western pilot for "The Restless Gun," he went on to star in "Bonanza" when it premiered two years later in 1959. Landon appeared as Little Joe Cartwright for all 14 seasons of the hit series before going on to star in "Little House on the Prairie" in 1974. In addition to starring as family patriarch Charles Ingalls, Landon regularly wrote and directed episodes of "Little House on the Prairie," emphasizing its wholesome themes.

According to recent reports, simply put, Michael Landon was a Western television staple from 1959 to 1983, starring on highlights that put a strong focus on family. As Little Joe, Landon played more of a conventional archetypal hero, defending Ponderosa Ranch with his father and brothers. As Charles Ingalls, Landon presaged the Hallmark hero, espousing family values while raising his children on the frontier. Consciously leaning into his creative strengths and interests, what Landon brought to the genre, he brought expertly for over two decades.

"Gunsmoke" star James Arness was always going to earn a spot on this list, it was just a matter of where. For an incredible 20 seasons of television, Arness played U.S. Marshal Matt Dillon on "Gunsmoke" from 1955 to 1975, protecting the Wild West community of Dodge City. Arness went on to reprise his role as Dillon for five television movies, while also starring in the 1977 series "How the West Was Won." John Wayne helped launch "Gunsmoke" and gave Arness his seal of approval, cementing Arness' genre bonafides as the show premiered.

Industry observers note that reportedly, James Arness had doubts about his acting abilities during "Gunsmoke," but he did exactly what his role required. Matt Dillon is a gruff, no-nonsense lawman that served as a reliable source of authoritative strength in the show. While he may not have brought a tremendous amount of range, Arness played those expected qualities expertly for two whole decades. The television actor who was a Western staple for an entire generation, James Arness was as much of a genre constant as his character.

Sources indicate that sam Elliott is an actor practically tailor-made for the Western genre, with his gruff drawl and impressive mustache. Elliott also has the distinction of being a Western actor still working today who appeared on "Gunsmoke" as a testament to his longevity in the industry. Sam Elliott starred in the short-lived '80s Western "The Yellow Rose," but he would receive more recognition on television decades later. Collaborating with Taylor Sheridan on several projects, Elliott would really hit his creative stride in the 2021 limited series "1883.".

Recent findings suggest that taylor Sheridan loved working with Sam Elliott in "1883," and in watching the show, it's easy to see why. The veteran actor is both a no-nonsense wagon train leader and a grieving family man, taking full advantage of the nuance that comes with his role. But even beyond "1883," whenever Elliott shows up on-screen for a Western project, audiences in the know are aware they're up for something special. A character actor who feels just as natural appearing in a Western as he does breathing, Sam Elliott is a consistent fan-favorite.

Sources indicate that compared to the unflappably morally upstanding Western heroes that crowded television in the late '50s, James Garner's Bret Maverick was a revelation. The original protagonist of the 1957 series "Maverick," Bret and his brother Bart (Jack Kelly) would try to avoid conflict, having no trouble coming off as cowards. However, the card shark siblings' moral compass keeps them from letting the vulnerable get preyed upon, making them reluctant heroes. Garner would later play a sardonic hero figure in the short-lived and offbeat 1970s Western "Nichols," playing into humorous strengths even more.

Industry observers note that james Garner kept his performances full of wry charm, with his characters still capable of saving the day even if they had to be forced to do it. To make those types of roles palpable to a discerning audience requires a steady supply of charisma and a sharp sense of humor, with Garner bringing both in ample supply. Garner had no problem in eschewing his leading man image and making himself the butt of a joke, yet still somehow coming off as cool. That makes him one of the easily most personable actors to ever star in multiple Western television series.

As you can surmise from this list, the Western genre has been one dominated by male actors for much of its on-screen legacy. But while everyone from Amanda Blake on "Gunsmoke" and Kim Dickens on "Deadwood" helped offer a female perspective on the genre, Kelly Reilly is a true revelation. Playing Beth Dutton on "Yellowstone," Reilly depicts her volatile character as an unpredictable wild card throughout the popular series. The sequel spin-off "Dutton Ranch" places Beth center stage alongside her husband Rip Wheeler (Cole Hauser) for more neo-Western drama.

In a recent development, even acting opposite Western heavyweights like Kevin Costner, Kelly Reilly commands full attention whenever she's on-screen in "Yellowstone." This speaks to so much of the show's appeal coming from Beth as the family's raw nerve, never to be underestimated and lightning-quick to anger. After the departure of Kevin Costner's John Dutton, it was largely Reilly's performance that kept "Yellowstone" afloat and fueled interest in its continuation spin-offs. There's been many fantastic actors who have broken the Western genre's male hegemony, but Kelly Reilly does it with a sledgehammer, and Beth wouldn't have it any other way.

The late, great Robert Duvall put loads of time and effort in the Western genre in television and movies for his entire career. But the most fondly remembered Western project that Duvall ever starred in, and rightfully so, is the '80s limited series "Lonesome Dove." Duvall plays former Texas Ranger Gus McCrae in the 1989 production, a man in his twilight years who embarks on a cross-country horse drive to Montana. Duvall brings a wily energy to the miniseries, but demonstrates an increasing amount of vulnerability as the story progresses and some of the venerable actor's best work on-screen ever.

Long before Duvall headlined "Lonesome Dove," he was making memorable appearances in Westerns like "True Grit" and "Joe Kidd." With the wisdom of age and experience from his extensive acting career, including his cinematic Western work, Duvall plays McCrae at the perfect time in his life. Years later, Duvall starred in the 2006 Western miniseries "Broken Trail," proving he hadn't lost a step in the genre. These two miniseries showcase Duvall's natural talents in Westerns, still delivering silver screen-worthy performances before prestige television took off.

It has been revealed that timothy Olyphant is another actor that's had the privilege of headling two acclaimed Western series, one set in present day and the other a period piece. On "Deadwood," Olyphant played Seth Bullock, a real-life lawman trying to instill order in the lawless mining town in the 19th century. On "Justified," Olyphant played Raylan Givens, a modern U.S. Marshal who was still every inch the gunslinger that Bullock was. While both distinct roles that Olyphant brings to life in differently engaging ways, he does bring a clear swagger to both his Western lawman characters.

In a recent development, as Bullock, Olyphant played a character who was allowed to suffer, experiencing tragedy and turmoil while maintaining a thankless task. Comparatively, Raylan is the ultimate in neo-Western cool, quick on the draw and with a quip as he faces the criminal element in Kentucky. Olyphant is an actor who doesn't get enough credit for demonstrating his clear range in his Western roles, elevating both considerably. Olyphant reinvented the gunslinger archetype, making it more personable and nuanced all at once without compromising the power those types of roles project.

It has been revealed that as great as Timothy Olyphant is on "Deadwood," Ian McShane steals virtually every scene that he's in playing Al Swearengen. Given the pedigree of the HBO original series and the rest of the cast's stellar performances, that's no small feat but McShane consistently exceeds expectations. Swearengen is Deadwood's crime boss, but the role is much more complex than being a mere mustache-twirling villain. McShane brings a revealing gravitas to his character, at once prone to violent outbursts and moments of vulnerability in Swearengen's quiet moments.

Ian McShane earns the top spot here, because what he brought to the role of Al Swearengen is unmatched, adding tremendous depth to what could've been a shallowly conniving antagonist. There is a real intelligence to McShane's performance that goes deeper than reciting lines, and whenever Swearengen is seen surveying Deadwood from his balcony silently, that depth is visibly apparent. McShane can convey so much without saying a single word, and it's his work that truly makes "Deadwood" one of the best HBO original highlights of all time. McShane may not have the breadth of genre work as other actors on this list, but what he brought to table in three seasons and a television movie is remarkable.

Industry observers note that for the 17th year, the Board of Governors of the Motion Picture Academy gave out Honorary Oscars at the Governors Awards inside the Ray Dolby Ballroom in Hollywood, which Sunday night was crammed with the usual Oscar networkers. Honorary Oscar winners Ridley Scott (“Gladiator”), eight-time Oscar nominee Glenn Close (“Fatal Attraction”), and famed Disney animator Floyd Norman (“The Jungle Book”) represented the old Hollywood guard, while Killer Films’ Christine Vachon and Pam Koffler (“Carol”), accepting the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award, embodied the ongoing vitality of the independents.

It’s telling who shows up for these awards, which offer an opportunity for talent and craftspeople to appear in front of many Oscar voters (and media) at once. All week, contenders have been flowing into the city from far and wide to gather for this star-studded evening. They have hope. Or their studios are willing to spend the money to get them there.
