Matt Damon, who has been working overtime this week on a series of “The Odyssey” panels (he moderated one), introduced Oscar honoree Ridley Scott and a stunning clip reel including “The Duellists,” “Blade Runner,” “Alien,” “Gladiator,” “Napoleon” and, of course, Damon’s “The Martian,” which he almost turned down because the role of an abandoned astronaut stranded in space seemed too similar to “Interstellar.” “Nobody gives a shit,” remarked Scott. Damon was glad he made “The Martian.” Scott, who is 88 and still working, sent his pre-recorded video acceptance from London. In it, he honored his late brother, “Top Gun” and “Crimson Tide” director Tony Scott, who died in 2012. “His great work would certainly have earned this recognition,” Scott said.

Of course, it didn’t hurt for Damon to charm the room as he vies for a Best Actor Oscar for his role as wily Odysseus in “The Odyssey.” Chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment Donna Langley’s table was packed with Damon and fellow contenders Christopher Nolan, Emma Thomas, Tom Holland, Zendaya, casting director John Papsidera, John Leguizamo, and more.

According to recent reports, and it didn’t hurt for John Malkovich to honor his old “Dangerous Liaisons” costar and Newly introduced York theater buddy Glenn Close at the same time that he is vying for Best Actor for Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight). “Numerous screenwriters and playwrights have uttered that phrase over the years: ‘made better by Glenn Close,'” he mentioned. “Glenn’s got the goods. She can do the major stuff, the little stuff, and everything in between.” Her list is long and includes eight nominations. She broke out in “The World According to Garp,” followed by “The Big Chill,” “The Natural,” “Mars Attacks,” “Albert Nobbs,” “The Wife,” “Hillbilly Elegy,” and more. The story of casting her in “Fatal Attraction” is legendary. After the studio resisted, fearing she was too wholesome, Close insisted on auditioning and blew Paramount chief Sherry Lansing and Michael Douglas away. On Sunday, Close was visibly moved accepting her prize, wiping away tears, while acknowledging past co-stars like Robin Williams and Malkovich, and departed champions such as her “World According to Garp” director George Roy Hill. “Look George, I got one,” she said, holding her Oscar up toward the heavens.

Last year’s Honoree Tom Cruise showed up to support not just box-office disaster “Digger” ($50 million worldwide, stratospheric budget), he told me, “but everyone.” Cruise still goes to see movies in theaters, sneaking in, he said, cap lowered. When he screens in his private screening room, it’s often when he wants to scrutinize a film and play it repeatedly. For his part, Oscar-winning director A.G. Iñárritu (“Birdman”) felt “confused,” he said, by the range of reactions to “Digger” (Metacritic: 46), which is not ranking high on Gold Derby charts. Production Design and Cinematography seem to be its best shots.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced Hollywood world order was on view. Early in the evening Langley was chatting with CAA’s Bryan Lourd but didn’t want to linger near the Warner Bros. table, where Skydance’s freshly minted Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz was eventually seated, while Denis Villeneuve presided over the “Dune: Part Three” table with Timothée Chalamet, who walked the red carpet with Kylie Jenner. Tom Quinn headed Neon’s table, which was front and center; producers David Heyman and Jennifer Fox, director Luca Guadagnino and stars Andrew Garfield and Yori Borisov represented Neon pickup “Artificial” (December 25). According to Fox, “Artificial” tested well before it was dropped by Amazon/MGM. Certainly the success of Silicon Valley documentary “You Can See Everything” (A24) bodes well. Quinn isn’t worried. And everyone has been asking Heyman about the hunt for the next James Bond. “We’ll know soon,” he said wearily. ENHANCEMENT: Indeed, Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three” star Rob Pattinson was declared Monday morning.

Industry observers note that james Gray sat with his “Paper Tiger” stars Adam Driver and Miles Teller, who snuck out before the end of the show. “Fjord” star Sebastian Stan hung with his director Cristian Mungiu, who is running an English-language film festival right before Cannes in Romania.

Netflix’s Ted Sarandos and latest content chief Peter Rice (who said he will not hire anyone to replace Dan Lim) commandeered several tables for its top contenders, “La Bola Negra” and “Possible Love.”.

It has been revealed that during the cocktail hour, I asked a couple of documentary branch members if still-buzzy “You Can See Everything” will land a nomination for their branch. “It’s competitive,” said one, citing “Naza” and “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” as shoo-ins. “They’ll get shortlisted.” Also in the mix is “Musk” director Alex Gibney, who flew in from Amsterdam — these days awards campaigns are international — and greeted his date, who had also flown in from Europe, musician David Byrne, who wrote a song for the movie. Gibney asked me to photograph him with his doppelganger, elegant “Wild Horse Nine” star John Malkovich. “People confuse me for him all the time,” said Gibney.

Many movie stars hugged and kissed, among them Garfield and Sophie Okonedo, who stars in two well-reviewed festival favorites this season, “Mouse” and “Clarissa.” Sandra Hüller, star of “Rose,” “Fatherland,” and “Project Hail Mary,” asked to be introduced to the belles of the Academy Ball, Killer Films producers Christine Vachon and Pam Koffler.

Recent findings suggest that there was warmth in the room for Scott, Norman, and Close, but the real whoops and cheers were saved for Vachon and Koffler. Filmmaker Todd Haynes, who met Vachon at Brown, introduced the duo along with Killer Films vet and Oscar-winner Julianne Moore (“Still Alice”), who is the current frontrunner for Best Actress for Jesse Eisenberg’s musical “The Debut.”.

“The Debut” opens December 11th, and will likely add to A24’s amazing year at the box office, with “The Invite,” “You Can See Everything,” “Club Kid,” “Primetime,” “The Drama,” “Tony,” and “Backrooms.”.

The Killer film list is long and varied and ranges over many transgressive subjects, including “Kids,” “Boys Don’t Cry,” “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,” “Far from Heaven,” “Still Alice,” “Carol,” and their first best Picture nomination, “Past Lives.” I nabbed a t-shirt listing their films in small type at their Saturday night Soho House party, which drew an impressive crowd: Sony Pictures Classics co-chiefs Tom Bernard and Michael Barker, John Turturro, Cinetic’s John Sloss, Academy documentary branch governor Roger Ross Williams, producers Cathy Schulman and Jon Kilik, Mubi’s Laura Kim, Strand’s Marcus Hu, filmmakers Lisa Cholodenko and Wash Westmoreland, and many more. (See our Killer Films story here.) Among the many collaborators they thanked at the Governors Awards for helping them over the years was PR stalwart Jeff Hill.

It wasn’t lost on the Academy crowd that while “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” kicked ass at the 2026 box office, the indies are flourishing at the moment, shooting original rockets into the system. Killer Films represents that energy. “Indie films, as we’ve seen this year, are as vital as ever,” Academy CEO Bill Kramer told me. “And Christine and Pam have led the way for decades and decades, and they’ve told stories that we had not seen before, and everybody’s responding to them again and again and again. These are films with staying power.”.

Industry News: The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence.
  • While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025.
  • “Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!).

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

It has been revealed that referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

Industry observers note that A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that the term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Industry observers note that depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a newly introduced TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—significant-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that indicates about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

During a recent interview with MovieZine while promoting Way of the Warrior Kid, the actor was asked whether he'd be interested in reuniting with Gunn for a fourth installment. He hadn't spoken to the filmmaker since the DC news broke, but his answer was encouraging:.

He directed all three movies, and that's pretty rare… so if he wanted to come back and bring it back, I would love that.

Well, now I want it too. Gunn spent nearly a decade building one of Marvel's strangest superhero teams into something audiences genuinely cared about. Somehow, he also made me cry over a talking raccoon more times than I'd care to admit.

This conversation is considerably less cheerful for DC fans. Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios following the Warner Bros. ownership shake-up, with former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham taking over Dec. 1, raising plenty of questions about the DC Universe's future.

It has been revealed that gunn isn't exactly sitting at home waiting for Marvel to call. He's still involved with Man of Tomorrow, his follow-up to 2025's Superman, which is scheduled for July 2027. He also has other DC-related work on his plate. Still, stepping away from running an entire studio should eventually give him more freedom to choose what he wants to direct. But does he want to direct a fourth GotG?

Pratt's comments are especially interesting because he previously had some pretty specific thoughts about returning as Star-Lord. Last year, I covered his concerns about finding somebody who could fill Gunn's shoes. At the time, it seemed unlikely the filmmaker would ever be available. Suddenly, that possibility doesn't sound quite so ridiculous.

It has been revealed that there's also the matter of where we left Peter Quill. At the end of Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, he returned to Earth to reconnect with his grandfather, while Rocket took charge of a fresh Guardians lineup. The movie's closing credits promised Star-Lord would return, though the powers that be haven't mentioned in what capacity or which new Marvel flick he might show up in.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Pratt recently confirmed there have been conversations about bringing him back, which is encouraging. Although returning for another Avengers movie and reuniting with Gunn for a fourth Guardians adventure would be two very different things. There's still no indication that Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 4 is actually happening. Gunn spent years saying the third movie would conclude his trilogy, and he may have no interest in revisiting those characters. I certainly wouldn't blame him for wanting to move on from comic book and superhero fare to something completely different. At this point, he's been helming superhero content for more than a decade. Maybe he wants to spread his wings and take on a different type of movie, which I would be stoked for as well.

It has been revealed that still, I love the idea of Pratt and Gunn finding their way back to each other, especially after everything they accomplished with the first three movies. Maybe it's wishful thinking, but if Gunn ever decides he's ready for another trip into space, I hope Marvel answers the phone.

The first three original Guardians of the Galaxy films are available to stream with a Disney+ subscription.

Still, I hope Amazon, new 007 director Denis Villeneuve, and the powers that be hear my plea: cast Stewart as Pattinson's first substantial Bond bad.

Tech Report: The Odyssey's Most Disturbing Scene Barely Used Any CGI. Here's How They Pulled It Off.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • She led them in, sat them on chairs, and blended them a potion of barley, cheese, and golden honey, mixed with Pramnian wine.
  • Industry observers note that christopher Nolan's The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that it's the kind of effect you'd assume required extensive computer-generated imagery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

She led them in, sat them on chairs, and blended them a potion of barley, cheese, and golden honey, mixed with Pramnian wine. She added potent drugs to make them totally forget their home. They took and drank the mixture. Then she struck them, using her magic wand, and penned them in the pigsty. They were turned to pigs in body and voice and hair; their minds remained the same. — The Odyssey, Emily Wilson translation.

Industry observers note that christopher Nolan's The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17, giving audiences another opportunity to experience the filmmaker's ambitious adaptation of Homer's epic poem. Among the story's many memorable encounters is Circe, a powerful sorceress who turns Odysseus' men into pigs. Played by Samantha Morton, Circe is responsible for one of the film's most unsettling sequences, which involves a human head being transformed into that of a pig.

Industry observers note that it's the kind of effect you'd assume required extensive computer-generated imagery. As it turns out, the filmmakers accomplished almost the entire transformation using practical effects, some silicone, and a few strategically placed magnets.

Speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson and special effects supervisor Scott Fisher explain how the sequence came together, revealing that the secret wasn't some elaborate digital trick. Instead, it was finding a way to let Morton perform the transformation herself.

I didn't understand at that point how much technology in that world has advanced.

Emma Thomas, Nolan's wife and longtime producing partner, admits that several moments in the screenplay left her wondering how they could possibly be accomplished, but the Circe sequence stood out.

"I loved that sequence when I read it, and I knew he wanted to make it feel very grounded," Thomas tells Polygon. "I knew that he wanted to try and do it with makeup effects to the extent that he could.".

Thomas wasn't initially sure how that would work, particularly given the limitations she assumed existed with practical makeup effects.

"I didn't understand at that point how much technology in that world has advanced," she claims.

Her confidence grew once she began meeting with the makeup, special effects, and visual effects teams, including makeup and creature effects artist Conor O'Sullivan.

"That was the point at which I really realized: Oh my goodness, these guys are gonna come up with a way that each can contribute their talents and their skills with the best of technology from within their own disciplines and make a seamless sequence.".

Of course, getting there required a little trial and error.

According to Jackson, the team knew early on that the key to the sequence would be allowing Morton to physically interact with the heads and manipulate their transformation.

"We had various ways that we were gonna try and achieve that, with heads with kind of clay layers that she could manipulate," Jackson indicates.

They even built some of those early versions, but the results weren't particularly promising. The transformation took too long, making the effect difficult to incorporate into the scene.

"We both were looking at it and going, 'Yeah, that's not really gonna work in Chris's world,'" Jackson recalled.

Sources indicate that rather than abandon the practical approach, the team came up with a different solution, working alongside O'Sullivan to develop a skull beneath a layer of soft silicone skin. The idea was that Morton could manipulate the skull through the skin, physically changing the shape of the head. But O'Sullivan had another trick up his sleeve.

"Conor came up with this great idea of having it pre-broken and stuck back together with magnets so she could do whatever kind of manipulation she wanted to and just keep going," Jackson says.

According to recent reports, the skull was already separated into pieces, with magnets holding everything together. That allowed Morton to squeeze and reshape the head as part of her performance, rather than wait for a complicated mechanical effect to do the work. And because the prop didn't require constant resetting, Morton could continue performing without interruption.

"The idea that there was no resetting, so no kind of breaking her performance, was why that scene was so compelling," Jackson says. "She just had this prop that she could really go to town on.".

It has been revealed that for an effect involving a human head becoming a pig's, giving an actor that kind of freedom might sound like a strange creative priority. But it meant the transformation wasn't simply something happening to a character through movie magic. Morton was physically making it happen.

"Ultimately, in what ended up in the film, there is very little visual effects affecting what was actually shot," Jackson notes.

Sources indicate that the visual effects team made some adjustments, including manipulating the eyeballs to make their movements more frantic. Jackson also notes that an ear transformation required combining two camera angles and slight of hand. But the majority of the sequence was accomplished in-camera.

In a recent development, "Essentially all our involvement was prior to the shoot, and then once the shoot happened, that was kind of it in camera," Jackson indicates. The visual effects team wasn't absent from the process. Its expertise helped develop the practical solution in the first place.

It's also consistent with Nolan's broader filmmaking philosophy, and the director notes that even sequences requiring visual effects benefit from capturing as much real material as possible.

Industry observers note that "Even where we know we're absolutely gonna have to avail ourselves of visual effects, really try to give the compositors as much as possible to work with," Nolan tells Polygon. In the case of Circe's transformation, that collaboration resulted in an effect that required very little digital assistance once filming was complete.

Sources indicate that for Thomas, the finished sequence demonstrates just how much could be accomplished when different effects departments combine their expertise. What initially seemed like one of the screenplay's biggest technical challenges became an example of practical and digital artists working together to find a solution.

Industry observers note that and for audiences revisiting The Odyssey at home, the sequence offers something worth examining a little more closely. Beneath all that unsettling movie magic is a surprisingly straightforward idea: a silicone-covered skull held together with magnets, and an actress given the freedom to do the rest.

The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that studios abandoned significant comedies years ago.
  • It has been revealed that as does 2008's "Role Models," which saw Rudd team up with Seann William Scott for a film that, like pretty much every comedy movie released at the time, was defined by the improvisational, R-rated humor that had made Apatow's films so successful.
  • Recent findings suggest that as someone who watched "Role Models" when it came out, I simply cannot believe this movie is 18 years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that studios abandoned significant comedies years ago. But in the 2000s and early 2010s, we really had it good. This was the age of the Judd Apatow comedy, in which the director not only delivered such modern classics as "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" and "Knocked Up," but influenced almost every comedy released during the era. Alongside the main Apatow offerings you had those which he produced such as "Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy," or those made by his collaborators, such as "Superbad." Then, there were those films that featured Apatow associates but were made without his direct involvement. The brilliant "I Love You, Man" is one example which, despite being criminally overlooked, remains one of Paul Rudd's best films.

It has been revealed that as does 2008's "Role Models," which saw Rudd team up with Seann William Scott for a film that, like pretty much every comedy movie released at the time, was defined by the improvisational, R-rated humor that had made Apatow's films so successful. This particular movie, however, paired Apatow allies Rudd and Christopher Mintz-Plasse with former members of sketch comedy troupe The State in director David Wain and writer/actor Ken Marino.

Recent findings suggest that as someone who watched "Role Models" when it came out, I simply cannot believe this movie is 18 years old. Despite being less well known than the aforementioned "Knocked Up" and its ilk, "Role Models" became instantly beloved by me and my friends upon its release. Almost two decades later, it's strange to think that an entire generation has grown up without films such as this shaping their sense of humor. If you happen to be part of that group, now's the time to acquaint yourself with this  oft-overlooked comedy. If, like me, you remember "Role Models" fondly, you'll be happy to hear it holds up.

Like so many of the best comedies of the 2000s, "Role Models" succeeds because despite being an R-rated comedy with frequent gross-out gags and unapologetically immature humor, it's also a surprisingly tender story with its heart in the right place.

Sources indicate that paul Rudd plays Danny who, alongside Seann William Scott's Anson Wheeler, works as a promoter for the energy drink "Minotaur." Danny feels deeply unfulfilled and has become deeply cynical as a result, spending most of his time correcting people on their speech. This causes his girlfriend, Beth (Elizabeth Banks), to break up with him, after which Danny loses it during a presentation at a high school. His freak out leads to both he and Anson being assigned to community service at Sturdy Wings, a big brother-style program where the pair become mentors to two "littles.".

According to recent reports, anson is paired with Ronnie (Bobb'e J. Thompson) a foul-mouthed kid with no friends, while Danny is given Augie Farks (Christopher Mintz-Plasse), a teenager obsessed with his medieval LARP group. At first, Danny and Anson are merely going through the motions. But over time they develop a bond with their "littles" — one which just might melt Danny's cold, cynical heart.

The secret star of "Role Models" is Joe Lo Truglio, who plays Kuzzik, a particularly dedicated LARP-er who, if you watch the bloopers, made it almost impossible for Rudd to get through any of his scenes without breaking. But there are a ton of standout performances here, from A.D. Miles as overly earnest Sturdy Wings counsellor Martin Gary to Ken Jeong as the self-serious LARP king Argotron and Jane Lynch as a former addict turned Sturdy Wings leader.

"Role Models" hit theaters in November 2008 and grossed a solid $92.6 million on a $28 million budget. It also garnered positive reviews, earning a 77% "certified fresh" rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Dana Stevens of Slate found "Role Models" to be "strewn with enough serendipities to make it a worthy variation on the dudes-grow-up genre," while the San Francisco Chronicle's Peter Hartlaub noted how, while Seann William Scott and Paul Rudd were "from two different moviemaking cliques" they ultimately "get along fine in a Bing Crosby/David Bowie kind of way.".

Meanwhile, Rafer Guzman of Newsday noted how Rudd, who co-wrote the script with David Wain, Timothy Dowling, and Ken Marino, had "clearly learned a few things working on Judd Apatow comedies." By that point, Rudd had appeared in Apatow's "The 40-Year-Old Virgin" and "Knocked Up," as well as several Apatow-produced projects including "Anchorman" and "Forgetting Sarah Marshall." As such, he was well-established as one of the most prominent figures of the 2000s R-rated comedy boom.

Industry observers note that but The State boys certainly brought their own flair to the film and the pairing of theirs and Rudd's sensibility along with Scott's lovable knucklehead charm made for a hilarious and surprisingly heartwarming experience that deserves to be remembered as fondly as some of the more well-known comedies of the era. If you fancy giving one of the most underrated buddy comedies of the 2000s another go, or are yet to see the "Role Models," the movie is available to watch for free on Pluto TV.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robert Pattinson is officially the man of the moment. 2026 was already his year, of course, considering his acclaimed turns in everything from A24's "The Drama" to Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" to "Primetime" — with still another massive appearance to come in December with "Dune: Part 3." That's on top of reprising his role as Bruce Wayne/Batman in Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II" and, as of today, his official casting announcement as James Bond. But can we take a moment to pour one out for the equally-as-talented character actor doomed to be the runner-up far more often than he deserves? We're talking, of course, about Nicholas Hoult.

It has been revealed that we've sort of been dreading this exact outcome the moment we first heard about the various finalists up for the world-famous MI6 agent. He's even waded into the blockbuster arena a few times, first in the 20th Century Fox "X-Men" movies and most recently as Lex Luthor in James Gunn's DC Universe.

It has been revealed that but, despite all that success, we have to point out how the "Mad Max: Fury Road" scene-stealer continues to get the short end of the stick. Adding insult to injury, this isn't even the first time he's watched Pattinson specifically land the coveted role he was eyeing. So here's to Nicholas Hoult, the perpetual underdog who'll always be a star in our hearts.

It has been revealed that "Always the bridesmaid, never the bride" is probably too harsh to describe what's going on with Nicholas Hoult lately but, man, it reaches a point. Despite proving himself to have one heck of a screen presence throughout the last several years, whether it be as an agent of chaos in Yorgos Lanthimos' "The Favourite" in 2018 or as a leading man in 2019's "Tolkien" biopic or even the horror-heavy "Nosferatu," Hoult has clearly been aching for the unambiguous breakout role that would make him a household name among general audiences. With all due respect to his meme-factory performances in "The Menu" or "Superman," well, neither of those have quite cut it. (Although that one photoshoot for "The Great" alongside Elle Fanning still leaves rent-free in our minds. You know the one.).

Industry observers note that sadly, that trend continues with the James Bond announcement. Real ones know it all started when Hoult was in contention for the title role in Matt Reeves' "The Batman," reportedly the only other name considered along with Robert Pattinson. But wait, it gets worse. After losing out on that crown jewel for superheroes, Hoult managed to find himself in the running for Superman a few short years later for James Gunn's reboot — which he ended up falling just short of, as well, though he picked up the role of supervillain Lex Luthor in a fun bit of meta casting. Third time isn't the charm, however, as he's now once again looking up to Pattinson as our newest Bond. How much is one man supposed to endure???

We love you, Nicholas Hoult, even if Hollywood's casting directors apparently have it out for you.

The Brits Are (Finally) Subverting the Cozy Crime Craze

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “I get it, because I love invoking that nostalgia, but I think that term also implies a certain ease,” Mark Gatiss recently explained to Variety his apprehension at the “cozy crime” label being applied to his latest labor of love.
  • As much a meditation on navigating sexuality in the immediate aftermath of World War II as a period procedural, Gatiss’ PBS series “Bookish” certainly has plenty to chew on.
  • Indeed, once the domain of Hallmark Channel, whose twee franchises (“Curious Caterer,” “Crossword Mysteries”) are as formulaic as their tradwife propaganda romances, the cozy crime drama is undergoing something of a commercial and creative renaissance of late.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “I get it, because I love invoking that nostalgia, but I think that term also implies a certain ease,” Mark Gatiss recently explained to Variety his apprehension at the “cozy crime” label being applied to his latest labor of love. “And doesn’t have to be just wallpaper; it can have teeth.”.

As much a meditation on navigating sexuality in the immediate aftermath of World War II as a period procedural, Gatiss’ PBS series “Bookish” certainly has plenty to chew on. In fact, alongside “Ludwig” and “Death Valley,” it’s leading the British charge to subvert a sub-genre widely dismissed as undemanding background fodder.

Indeed, once the domain of Hallmark Channel, whose twee franchises (“Curious Caterer,” “Crossword Mysteries”) are as formulaic as their tradwife propaganda romances, the cozy crime drama is undergoing something of a commercial and creative renaissance of late. According to a recent study, 75 percent of 18-29 year-olds, a generation embracing everything ASMR to knitting to drown out the noise, consider themselves fans. Related Stories ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters.

“Bookish” centers on Gatiss’ Gabriel Book, a secondhand bookseller in post-war London who — thanks to a mysterious letter signed by Winston Churchill — is entrusted to apply his encyclopedic knowledge with the Met Police. Yet while its 1940s setting, killing methods (poisoned bonbons) and great British fondness for the cuppa (“Without tea, I am merely reconstructed dust,” Book declares) may be the stuff of Agatha Christie, its themes are unusually progressive.

For Book is also in a lavender marriage with Polly Walker’s strong independent woman Trottie, explaining why beyond his remarkable sleuthing abilities, he remains something of a buttoned-up enigma. Laced with an air of melancholy, the series quietly but effectively delves into the hardships of staying in the closet at a time when homosexuality was still 20 years away from decriminalization, while also exploring the concept of platonic love, the disillusionment of women forced to retreat from the workplace, and the PTSD suffered by returning soldiers. A Lacey Chabert vehicle this is not.

As its Best Comedy win at the International Emmys would suggest, fellow two-season wonder “Ludwig” is slightly more jovial. In fact, it compels far more as a tragic-comic character study than a murder-mystery, its tendency to withhold vital information until the last-minute ensuring it’s practically impossible for armchair detectives to play along.

As the corduroy-clad, socially-awkward puzzle maker, David Mitchell essentially plays David Mitchell; no bad thing, of course, as his hilarious victory on “LOL UK” proved. Much of the BritBox show’s joys derive from watching a bumbling introvert, who poses as his detective twin brother to investigate his disappearance only to become the force’s secret weapon, struggling to adapt to center stage and the complexities of modern life. From his inability to make small talk to his near-pathological dislike of all mod-cons, Ludwig is a reluctant hero and, at times, an impenetrable one, too. (“Whichever one didn’t do it knows that the other one did and is protecting her. While the one that did do it knows we can’t prove that the one who didn’t do it, didn’t do it”).

It has been revealed that however, as with “Bookish,” creator Mark Brotherhood balances Ludwig’s quips and idiosyncrasies with a genuine sense of longing, not only for his missing sibling, but for the dad who abandoned them as youngsters as well as the sister-in-law he obviously holds a torch for. Come for the cryptic capers, stay for the complex family dynamics and post-millennial tensions.

Also returning to BritBox for its second season this month (out November 17), “Death Valley” is undeniably the most meta of the three, fully leaning into all the tropes — amateur sleuths unfathomably allowed to permeate crime scenes carte blanche, picture-perfect visuals which double up as tourist board ads (in this instance, the scenic Vale of Glamorgan), a distinct lack of blood, cursing or anything that shatters the illusion of a stiff-upper-lip utopia — while simultaneously skewering them in a blatant case of “have your cake and eat it.”.

Here, BAFTA nominee Timothy Spall plays John Chapel, a curmudgeonly reclusive “thespian with a capital T” best known for starring in a long-running cozy crime drama, Caesar, and his uber-corny catchphrase, “Crime waits for no man.” Brought out of hibernation when “scintillatingly irritating” fangirl DS Janie Mallowan (Gwyneth Keyworth) knocks on his door while investigating a nearby murder, he subsequently ingratiates himself into the inquiry, drawing upon his fictional experiences and celebrity ego to forge an unlikely — and often reluctant — buddy duo.

Sources indicate that there are inevitable parallels with “Only Murders in the Building” where Steve Martin’s Charles, the similarly jaded star of a classic detective show, also finds a fresh lease of life by teaming up with a younger woman to solve very real crimes. Instead of an overarching mystery rooted within a swanky high rise in Manhattan’s Upper West Side, though. “Death Valley” is a case-of-the-week affair grounded in the humdrum of rural South Wales: murder scenes include a rugby club, fish and chip shop, and community service litter-picking session.

Industry observers note that furthermore, the forays into showbiz are hardly dripping with glamour. Chapel briefly returns to his old day job not in a prestige reboot of his biggest hit, but a local amateur dramatic staging of “Hamlet.” Meanwhile, the fantasy series he infiltrates while investigating the death of a production runner looks hokier than a Syfy original.

Of course, the dichotomy between Chapel’s overinflated sense of self and the humbling situations he finds himself in provides much of the comedy. Despite admitting that cozy crime isn’t his bag, Spall is clearly having a ball as a luvvie prone to grand soliloquies about his craft and unwarranted pats on the back about his “revelatory Tartuffe at the Almeida.”.

Perhaps sensing the response from hardened critics scoffing at the absence of tortured souls and gritty visuals that leave you reaching for your remote’s contrast button, writer Paul Doolan also beats them to the punch with a string of self-knowing lines, whether Janie describing her partner’s performance as “hammy” or a prime suspect’s assertion that their whodunit reveal was “needlessly theatrical.”.

“Death Valley” is undeniably ‘played to the rafters.’ However, its smart self-deprecation and popculture-spoofing ensures that, like its counterparts, it rises above what Chapel himself calls “the current level of banality in most mainstream TV drama.” Isn’t that better than cozy?

The next massive question on a lot of James Bond fans' minds, now that Robert Pattinson has been named the next Bond, is who will play the next “Bond Girl”? Though the rumors and anticipation haven’t quite reached the fevered pitch that the Bond casting rumors did, there is still plenty of speculation out there. My feeling on it is that it could be one of the frontrunners, like Sydney Sweeney or Margaret Qualley, but it’s just as likely to be a name we’ve not heard yet. With all that said, let’s get into some of the rumors.

Looking at the prediction markets like Kalshi, the leader right now to be the next Bond Girl is Margaret Qualley in the yet-untitled Bond 26. As of today, she’s sitting at about 60% odds to nab the role. This is after coming on strong in recent weeks, after Sydney Sweeney had been the favorite for months. Sweeney’s odds have dropped to about 10% recently, but I still think she should be considered a serious contender, given her trajectory over the last few years.

In a recent development, the only other actresses above 20% are Ana Taylor-Joy (25%) and Florence Pugh (20%). These rumors make a lot of sense, actually. Like Pattinson, they have both worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve in the Dune series. It has been revealed that that goes for Zendaya, too, who is at the moment sitting at 17% on Kalshi, but she seems less likely to me. Other names who appear on the list include Daisy Edgar-Jones, Jodie Comer, Emma Mackey, Alicia Vikander, and Vanessa Kirby. The final name on the current list is also an interesting one: Ana de Armas. She worked with Villeneuve on Blade Runner 2049, and she’s been in a James Bond movie before, playing a fellow spy in No Time to Die. That could make for an interesting dynamic.

According to recent reports, so those are the top names on the prediction markets, but could it be someone else completely? Possible. These are pure speculation on my part, but how about Inde Navarrette? Her star is on the rise after her excellent performance in the surprise smash Obsession earlier in the 2026 movie schedule. She’s definitely someone to watch and could definitely draw some attention from the Bond producers, though she is scheduled to play Rogue in the 2028 X-Men movie, so she might not be available.

Recent findings suggest that what about Jenna Ortega? She’s promptly becoming one of the biggest stars in the world (despite a recent stumble with Klara and the Sun) with her roles in Wednesday and the Scream franchise and could be a great fit for the role. Chloë Grace Moretz, someone else who has played Wednesday Addams, is another possibility. Someone like Sadie Sink would make a great Bond Girl, too. Though, like Navarrette, she may be tied up in the MCU franchise for the foreseeable future.

So what does the future hold? Let the speculation begin!

Recent findings suggest that these headphones don’t have ANC, just passive isolation, but they still deliver solid sound, comfort, and strong battery life. They use physical controls and support one-touch pairing with most Apple devices, as well as hands-free Siri.A The Solo 4 headphones are compatible with Bluetooth 5.3 and work with the AAC and SBC codecs. The headphones last around 50 hours per charge (about 10 hours longer than their predecessor), and 10 minutes of charging gives you around five hours of playback, with a full recharge taking approximately two hours. Although they lack ANC and adjustable EQ, these headphones still have plenty of extra features for Apple users, and those shortcomings are much easier to forgive at almost 66% off. For $69, the Beats Solo 4 headphones are a compact and well-equipped option for casual listening, with long battery life and that classic Beats aesthetic.

‘Fast & Furious’ Meets ‘RoboCop’ in This Forgotten Sci-Fi Action Series

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in the 1980s and early '90s, if an action TV series wanted to succeed, the easiest way to do it was to give the hero a cool car.
  • '80s action TV got so wild that Airwolf went a step higher and made the vehicular hero a helicopter.
  • The Dodge Viper reached buyers in 1992.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in the 1980s and early '90s, if an action TV series wanted to succeed, the easiest way to do it was to give the hero a cool car. The Dukes of Hazzard had a Dodge Charger, Michael Knight (David Hasselhoff) drove around in a black Trans Am named KITT on Knight Rider, and in Magnum P.I., Thomas Magnum (Tom Selleck) looked like the coolest dude in the world behind the wheel of his bright red Ferrari.

'80s action TV got so wild that Airwolf went a step higher and made the vehicular hero a helicopter. Developed for CBS in 1993, Viper tried to recreate that success. Viper's plot was about a crime fighter who battles the bad guys while driving the new Dodge Viper sports car. Think Fast & Furious meets RoboCop, with a transforming vehicle doing the heavy lifting. There was only one problem: famed producer Stephen J. Cannell came up with a series carrying the exact same name.

The Dodge Viper reached buyers in 1992. It was a pricey sports car that not many could afford, but with its open roof, long hood, and wide front, it really did look like a viper ready to strike. A car like that might not be a huge seller on the mainstream market, but the style could surely be used to make money in other ways. Chrysler and Paramount Television worked on a deal that would make the Dodge Viper the star in its own titular CBS series simply called Viper.

Four people, four completely different ways of being somebody's family. Here is your seat at the table, what the rest of them would rely on you for, and the thing you would have to watch.

Recent findings suggest that you are the head of the table, and you did not ask for the job so much as end up holding it. Dom is the gravity of this franchise, which is why the films work best when everybody else is circling around whatever he has decided.

You are the one who notes the thing out loud and then does not take it back. Letty is the least sentimental person at that table and somehow the most loyal, which is a combination almost nobody manages.

You are the reason anybody remembers the night. Roman talks first, thinks second and is far more frightened than he lets on, which is precisely what makes him the most human person in the whole family.

In a recent development, you are the one who made the strategy work while everybody else was busy being heroic about it. Tej does not need the credit, which is fortunate, because in this family the credit tends to go to whoever drove fastest.

Sources indicate that the premise for the TV action series was simple: in the fictional Metro City, crime is running rampant, leading to the police department forming a crime-fighting force known as the Viper Project. At the center of this was a bright red Dodge Viper that could turn into a militaristic, silver, armored car called "Defender." The series would be led by James McCaffrey as Michael Payton (Viper's version of Michael Knight), and the car's creator and the brains behind the operation, the paralyzed Julian Wilkes (Dorian Harewood).

However, the same year that Viper was set to debut, another show with the exact same title went into production. This one was led by TV producer and novelist Stephen J. Cannell, the legend who helped create iconic TV shows such as The Rockford Files, The A-Team, and 21 Jump Street. Both series had similar premises, with a cool hero behind the wheel of a cool car called a Viper as they took down the bad guys, but only Paramount had the rights to use the actual Dodge Viper. This led to the Chrysler Corporation trying to stop Cannell Studios Inc. from going into production with their Viper series through a trademark infringement lawsuit.

Chrysler contended that the red car being used in trademarks for Cannell's Viper looked very similar to the Dodge Viper. It wasn't going to be an easy task to stop it, as Cannell's show had already cast Michael Dudikoff in the lead and sold the syndicated series to over 50 stations. A month later, Cannell Studios caved by changing the name of their Viper to Cobra and making the car an old-school Shelby Cobra.

Cobra premiered in September 1993 with Michael Dudikoff playing Robert "Scandal" Jackson, an A.W.O.L. Navy SEAL hiding out in Alaska who becomes an underground crime fighter for the secret organization Cobra while barreling through the fictional Bay City in his cherry red Shelby Cobra (what a coincidence!). Sadly, Cobra, which co-starred James Tolkan (best known as the principal in Back to the Future) as Cobra director Dallas Cassell, and Allison Hossack as Danielle LaPoint, Dallas' daughter and Scandal's partner, only lasted one season, going off the air in May 1994.

Industry observers note that although Viper was no huge hit, it fared much better than Cobra. Viper ended up premiering on NBC instead of CBS in January 1994, only to be canceled by the network after one season. That could have been the end of it, but Viper survived, returning for a second season in syndication in 1996. However, it was with an almost entirely newly introduced cast, now with a CIA agent named Thomas Cole (Jeff Kaake) leading the Viper group.

After two seasons with Kaake as the lead, James McCaffrey returned for the fourth and final season, now switching things up by driving a blue Dodge Viper. Fittingly, the series ended in the spring of 1999, the perfect time capsule of late 20th-century action television in an era before the landscape completely changed and left the simple but effective use of cool cars behind.

Industry News: What Makes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time So Great Anyway?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, spend even a little time online in gaming circles, and you'll inevitably come across claims that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the greatest games ever made.
  • Industry observers note that like most video games whose stories endure, Ocarina of Time blends elements of classic narrative styles.
  • Ghosts haunt Hyrule field, and fresh, stronger monsters lurk in places that young Link once played in safely, without a worry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spend even a little time online in gaming circles, and you'll inevitably come across claims that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the greatest games ever made. Those claims resurfaced with greater frequency with the announcement of the Nintendo Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake and subsequent warm reception from critics. The reaction from those I know who played for the first time and enjoyed it has generally been "yes, it really is one of the greats." What there's been less of, however, is a concerted effort to explain what exactly makes it deserving of that praise. Make no mistake, it does deserve it — and not just for reasons of nostalgia. That’s because Ocarina of Time anticipated some of gaming's biggest trends, and now that those trends have spiralled out of control, the remake serves as a blueprint for good game design moving forward.

Industry observers note that like most video games whose stories endure, Ocarina of Time blends elements of classic narrative styles. It's a fairy tale tinged with tragedy, a coming-of-age tale, and a remix of classic archetypes all mashed up together, and it's one of the few games that uses its game-ness to help tell that story. The landscape of Link's adult life changes dramatically, in obvious ways like all his friends scattering and various tragedies befalling Hyrule's people, but also in more mundane ways that drive a sharp distinction between past and present.

Ghosts haunt Hyrule field, and fresh, stronger monsters lurk in places that young Link once played in safely, without a worry. Grown Link can ride a horse. He wears clothes his child self would never have managed, uses tools too substantial for a kid, and is a master of combat arts. Liked the slingshot? Tough luck, buddy. That's for kids. Adults use real projectile weapons. These tools and the addition of a horse to Link's circle of friends give him access to new parts of Hyrule he never could've visited as a child — partly for reasons of geography, but also for the simple fact that he wouldn't have stood a chance against an angry Gerudo in his younger days.

These changes create a satisfying sense of progression, sure, but they're also one of the only examples of a coming-of-age story told through gameplay. Normally, such tales get their message across through some personal ordeal, or cumulative learning, or a big epiphany. But Link has a limited personality, so those methods wouldn’t work here. Instead, coming of age for Link means literally navigating the landscape of adulthood and adjusting to the newly introduced opportunities and limitations it presents, while the memory of childhood is never allowed to fade. No other game combined its storytelling and interactive elements in such a way when Ocarina of Time first introduced. Few have done it since, and none as successfully.

But Ocarina of Time was ahead of its time in more than just storytelling. It sits in the Goldilocks Zone between linearity and open-endedness. Ocarina won't hold your hand, but its relatively small size and contained nature mean you're bound to eventually work out the right path in a dungeon or the answer to a riddle on your own. It also means you're bound to run across some of its less immediately obvious side quests simply by chance, just from talking to people or investigating peculiarities in the environment. The lack of signposting creates an emergent feel that puts Ocarina closer to the likes of Disco Elysium than it does other action-adventure games of the '90s and, admittedly, most other rigidly designed modern games that fear you'll miss a side quest or line of dialogue if you aren't told where to look.

Industry observers note that ocarina’s rewards are usually small and limited, or sometimes just plain goofy. The tasks they're associated with demand comparatively little time, and the effort involved is effort engaging with the world — exploring out-of-the-way places, speaking with people, piecing together vague environmental clues — not clearing huge challenges or gathering dozens of unnecessary collectibles.

Sources indicate that you can sell four masks from the vendor in Hyrule Castle Town and get a fifth fun-but-impractical mask for your trouble, without feeling like that reward massively disrespects your time. It's fine that the hole in the ground on Death Mountain only houses a cow (questionable from an animal ethics standpoint, perhaps, but fine otherwise) because it took you under one minute to reach this point from elsewhere on the map. The existence of a secret underground cow is reward enough in itself. The practical side of it, some restorative milk for an empty bottle, is a nice bonus. Nintendo built Ocarina of Time around curiosity and a drive for exploration. It was the pinnacle of open-ended design at the time, and a philosophy driven by fun over content is something modern game developers are only just gradually rediscovering now.

Recent findings suggest that the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is timeless. It's a standout example of creativity in a contained scope and a rare instance where video games embrace what distinguishes them from other mediums and puts it to good use. Nostalgia might encourage fond feelings toward it, but it has a lot to offer beyond that and should serve as a guidepost for good game development moving forward.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that robert Pattinson has spent his career ping-ponging between major franchise fare ("Harry Potter," "Twilight," "The Batman") and weird arthouse fare ("The Lighthouse," "Good Time," "Cosmopolis"). Along the way, he's garnered a pretty broad fanbase, so there are plenty of people celebrating the news that Pattinson will be taking over the role of James Bond.

In a recent development, there were several other finalists to play the next Bond, including Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden, and Nicholas Hoult, but Pattinson was the clear frontrunner even before he was unveiled. Early reactions to the news have noted the somewhat absurd flex of landing the role of James Bond just a few years after landing the role of Batman. "This is the greed they talk about in the Bible," wrote one user on Reddit.

It has been revealed that casting such a well-known actor in the role of Bond bucks the trend of 007 casting, with previous revamps traditionally favoring actors who weren't already firmly established. Many people, while not necessarily disliking the choice of Pattinson for the role, have pointed out that Amazon isn't exactly taking a risk. Other Reddit consumers describe Pattinson as "a very conservative choice" and "very safe casting," with one wryly commenting, "This isn't beating the allegations of 'every movie has the same five actors in it.'" So, while casting a lesser-known actor would surely have attracted some controversy in its own right, some Bond fans feel that the safety of this choice is "disappointing.".

Sources indicate that and, of course, there are Batman fans who fear that this fresh commitment spells the end of Pattinson's tenure as the Dark Knight. Between production delays on "The Batman II," a recent power shake-up at DC Studios, and now this 007 casting news, the general assumption is that Pattinson's Batman will be hanging up his cape after two movies.

One of the upsides of having such an eccentric career and personality is that Robert Pattinson has generated a great many memes over the years — and now they're being put to good use. One Tumblr user adapted a famous "Twilight" scene to have Pattinson's Edward Cullen saying, "This is the skin of a [license to kill]er," Bella." Others, meanwhile, have joked that we "finally have a Gen Z James Bond," in reference to a Vanity Fair interview wherein Pattinson doggedly insists that he is Gen Z and that the year he was born "doesn't matter.".

One meme that became popular even before Pattinson was officially cast imagines the reactions of the other hopefuls auditioning for the role when they see the unstoppable Pattinson walk in after them.

every other actor when robert pattinson indicates up to audition pic.twitter.com/40fHsnS2C4.

Industry observers note that fans are particularly amused by the fact that Pattinson revealed up "late" to the audition process (which has been going on for years), sandwiching it in between his commitments to "Dune: Part Three" and "The Batman Part II," and still landed the role. But that kind of effortless swagger only makes him more perfect for the role of James Bond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Landman is paying off one of its longest-running arcs in season 3.

Created by Taylor Sheridan and Christian Wallace, the Paramount+ series following the work of Billy Bob Thornton's Tommy Norris in the oilfields of West Texas has been a strong hit for the streamer since its debut, frequently charting on its Top 10, even while some division has been directed towards certain elements of its writing. Its continued success netted Landman a season 3 renewal partway through season 2's airing, with filming getting underway in September 2026.

Industry observers note that as production continues on the next chapter of Taylor Sheridan's hit series, the Fort Worth-based Star-Telegram has unveiled upcoming set images from Landman season 3. The photos come from the show filming at TCU's Amon G. Carter Stadium during their game against Kansas State, and featured Michelle Randolph's Ainsley cheerleading alongside the rest of the team's squad, confirming her to finally be fulfilling her dream of performing on the field. The official TCU Athletics social media also offered official looks at Ainsley's cheerleading debut, as seen below:.

Recent findings suggest that when Ainsley is first introduced in Landman season 1, she's depicted as the stereotypical high school cheerleader, dating star quarterback Dakota and planning to apply to the University of Alabama to join him after he's offered a position with their team. As Sheridan's show progressed, however, Randolph's character has evolved into finding an identity of her own, including going to TCU, generally away from her mother and father, who are in the midst of reconciling.

In a recent development, the one thing that has stayed consistent is her desire to continue being a cheerleader beyond high school, with the start of Landman season 2 seeing her effectively securing a walk-on spot with TCU's team. However, with the season only picking up approximately six weeks after its predecessor, it also left Ainsley outside the normal college football season, therefore following her training and bonding with her fellow team members.

Beyond just showcasing her general debut as a TCU cheerleader, the upcoming Landman season 3 set photos also seem to point to Ainsley better getting along with her roommate, Bobbi Salvör Menuez's Paigyn. The non-binary character and Norris infamously butted heads for much of season 2 due to the former's more demanding behavior regarding their dorm room, eventually pushing Ainsley to move out and consider getting a place with her mom, Ali Larter's Angela. However, after an incident involving transphobic bullies, season 2 ended with the pair agreeing to try being roommates again.

Given Paigyn is part of the TCU sports medicine crew, it's very likely their inclusion could stem from that more so than them and Ainsley getting along better. Even still, with the Landman season 3 set photos looking to be celebratory for all the characters involved, Sheridan may have more lighthearted aims in store for the two as they overcome their initial differences to be friends.

Set in West Texas, Landman explores the world of oil rigs and the fortunes they create, with a modern upstairs/downstairs narrative of roughnecks and billionaires, highlighting the profound impact on the climate, economy, and geopolitics in these boomtowns.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that robert Pattinson is your new James Bond. Denis Villeneuve has cast Pattinson as the star in his 007 movie for Amazon MGM Studios. He will now be the seventh actor to officially star in the franchise and will lead what will be the 26th James Bond movie to hit the massive screen.

Villeneuve is directing Bond 26 from a script by Steven Knight, and the franchise is being guided by mega producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, who took over from the long-time stewards of 007, Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, upon the rights to Bond being acquired by Amazon following its acquisition of MGM.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime. I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team,” mentioned Robert Pattinson. Pattinson this year starred in “The Drama” and “Primetime” at A24, and is presently in production on Matt Reeves’ “The Batman Part II.” Last year’s credits included “Die My Love” opposite Jennifer Lawrence and “Mickey 17,” from Bong Joon Ho.

According to recent reports, “Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond as we proudly introduce Robert Pattinson as the next 007,” mentioned Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios. “This iconic character has captivated audiences around the world for more than six decades, and there’s no doubt that Robert’s remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice to carry that legacy forward. With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing, Tanya Lapointe executive producing, and a brilliant script from Steven Knight, we have a world-class creative team in place to usher in a fresh era of Bond, and we couldn’t be more excited about the journey ahead.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Few films carry the kind of anticipation that comes with James Bond, and we have strived to honor the passionate fans, the legacy, and the future of this iconic character. We are thrilled to officially welcome Robert Pattinson as our 007 and are confident he will bring something truly special to this role. Robert, Denis, Amy, David, and Tanya are embarking on an amazing adventure together,” said Courtenay Valenti, head of film at Amazon MGM Studios.

It has been revealed that “Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” stated director Denis Villeneuve.

According to recent reports, “James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies. The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times,” said producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.

Recent findings suggest that it’s been well over a year of fervent speculation as to whom would take up the mantle as Britain’s top super spy, as Villeneuve was unveiled to be taking the directing job way back in June 2025. Rumors abounded about who could star, with reports about a sprawling wish list and group of young Brits who had tested for the part. Film chief Courtenay Valenti teased the upcoming Bond movie at this year’s CinemaCon but noted “it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly” and would share more when the time was right. And with Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part 3” finally arriving this December, that time appears to be now.

The 26th Bond will be the first James Bond movie since 2021’s “No Time to Die,” which was the fifth and final entry for Daniel Craig as 007. That film, directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga, earned $774.1 million worldwide in its initial release (a UK re-release grossed another $132 million), putting it among the highest-grossing Bond movies ever, even when adjusted for inflation. The 25 films dating back to the ’60s have grossed $7.6 billion at the box office worldwide.

  • According to recent reports, shortly after its debut, Julian Fellowes' The Gilded Age joined the ranks of HBO reveals that got the world talking.
  • While The Gilded Age fans are concerned over Marian and Larry, Peggy and William have officially tied the knot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers ahead for the most recent episode of The Gilded Age.

According to recent reports, shortly after its debut, Julian Fellowes' The Gilded Age joined the ranks of HBO reveals that got the world talking. The show's fourth season began a few weeks ago on the network (and streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and there have already been a number of memorable moments. The third episode featured Peggy's marriage to Dr. William Kirkland, and Audra McDonald as well as executive producer Erica Armstrong Dunbar spoke about the importance of having the newlyweds jump the broom onscreen.

While The Gilded Age fans are concerned over Marian and Larry, Peggy and William have officially tied the knot. In a conversation with People, McDonald spoke remarked "it meant everything" for the series to show the upcoming pair jumping the broom onscreen, highlighting similar opinions to her character Dorothy. In the Broadway legend's words:.

Industry observers note that we’re honoring those traditions. We’re celebrating those traditions. We are shouting into the world who we are. I think that’s why it was crucial to Dorothy and Arthur [John Douglas Thompson], and especially because that was their broom, the one that they jumped over.

For those unfamiliar, jumping the broom is a wedding ceremony that goes back antebellum period in the United States. While enslaved people couldn't legally get married, couples would jump over a broom together to symbolize their union. It's remained a tradition for Black Americans in the years that followed, continuing to this day.

It has been revealed that jumping the broom became a point of contention leading up to Peggy's wedding, with her mother-in-law Elizabeth Kirkland (Phylicia Rashad) protesting its place in high society. Later in the same interview, Audra McDonald spoke more about why Dorothy and the entire Scott family was so passionate about it being included in the wedding ceremony, offering:.

[It meant that] our family is going to continue. That’s another thing. We didn’t know about the Scotts, how we were going to make it, especially with all the trauma that they went through, that we’re going to continue as a unified family. Now we have the possibility of future generations.

Indeed, the Scott family has come a long way since Season 1 of The Gilded Age. Despite trauma and issues, Peggy and her parents have found their way back to each other throughout the last three seasons. It was actually the same broom that Dorothy and Arthur jumped over before they were able to legally marry, making Peggy's use of the ceremony a full circle moment for the entire family.

According to recent reports, in the official Gilded Age podcast, Dr. Erica Armstrong Dunbar spoke about having Peggy and her husband jump the broom in Episode 4. As she put it:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Recent findings suggest that we had lots of conversation about jumping the broom. Julian Fellowes was very invested in the idea of showing what's become a very kind of popular connection to the past. And if you go to Black weddings today people jump the broom. I jumped the broom at my own wedding. But I'm a historian. And so we had lots of conversations because in the 1880s nobody's really jumping the broom.

Season 4 of The Gilded Age has been changing the dynamics of various characters, and Peggy is no exception. On top of being published writer, she's now a married woman in good standing with society. Having her jump the broom honored the character's history, and also had the opportunity to educate fans who might not know about this tradition. As she the show's EP continued:.

Arthur, who was enslaved and we established that since Season 1, and Dorothy did jump over a broom in their wedding. So there's a world in which it could have been passed down to Peggy. And knowing who Peggy is, of course she would want to honor that tradition no matter the discomfort that it gave to her soon-to-be in-laws... It was for the Kirklands a reminder of slavery that they found undignified and unwilling to have in the wedding of their son.

Sources indicate that ultimately the Kirklands ended up relenting, and Peggy and William jumping in the broom in a beautifully shot sequence of their nuptials. We'll just have to wait and see how Peggy's relationship with her in-laws changes now that they're officially family.

According to recent reports, newly introduced episodes of The Gilded Age air Sundays on HBO as part of the 2026 TV schedule. The season's drama is heating up, and I can't wait to see what comes next for this ensemble cast.
